idiom_name: dynamic import() + name-keyed registry (module cache means no unload)
implementation_notes: The classic structure collapses: the configuration is a JSON/JS object, the repository is a Map from component name to the awaited import() of a module specifier, and the loader is import() itself - an asynchronous function that returns a promise of the module namespace object and never throws synchronously. Nothing is ever unloaded: a successfully evaluated module stays in the module registry for the lifetime of the realm (MDN notes only evaluation failures may be retried), so replacing a component means a new worker/process or a versioned specifier. Node's module.register() hooks can customise resolution and loading but cannot evict modules, and the older require()+registry idiom is the same bargain inside CommonJS.
pitfalls: import() never unloads: deleting the registry entry leaves the module and all of its state in the module map, so a changed component needs a new worker/process (or a cache-busting specifier) - the biggest mismatch with the POSIX mental model.

Specifiers computed from configuration defeat static analysis: bundlers cannot resolve a variable specifier, so the import graph has to be declared (literal imports per component, or a glob such as Vite's import.meta.glob) or the production build silently omits the component.

In browsers a dynamic import obeys the same CORS, MIME and path rules as any module fetch; failures are asynchronous rejections, and only evaluation failures are cached, so retry behaviour differs between 'module not found' and 'module threw'.
